food.text: Sweet potato became a staple food, especially in Hawaii, Easter Island and New Zealand. By the 17th century in central Polynesia, traditional cultivars were being replaced with hardier and larger varieties from the Americas.

The leading theory holds that sweet potato first reached Polynesia from the west coast of South America around 1000 AD. Around 1500 AD, Spanish galleons and Portuguese traders introduced two more lineages, the Central American camote and the Caribbean batata. These later superseded the original kumara lineage.

In 1778, Captain James Cook arrived at the island of Niihau and left livestock and seeds behind. He gave the islanders a ram goat, ewes, a boar and an English sow, along with seeds for melons, pumpkins and onions.

In Ancient Hawaii, in the pre-contact period that lasted until 1778, men did all of the cooking. Food for women was cooked in a separate imu, or earth oven, and afterwards men and women ate their meals separately.

During the 1600s, traditional Polynesian cultivars of sweet potato and calabash began to be replaced with North American varieties. When the sweet potato was reintroduced, it had become entirely absent from many central Polynesian islands. One example is the Cook Islands, with the exception of Mangaia.
In 1793, Captain George Vancouver brought the first cattle to the Hawaiian Islands. They were longhorns from California, and they were presented to King Kamehameha I.

In Hawaii, the sweet potato (ʻuala) was considered less valuable than taro. It was still commonly grown because it could flourish in less favourable conditions and took only three to six months to mature.
Captain George Vancouver introduced grape vines to the Hawaiian Islands around 1792. This was about a year before he brought the first cattle to the islands in 1793.

Many Hawaiian māla (cultivations) mixed sugarcane (kō) with sweet potato. Sugarcane was planted in rows alongside the stone field walls to act as a windbreak for the sweet potatoes growing between the rows. The sweet potatoes were often planted in mounds, with the soil mulched with a mix of rocks and plants.

Sweet potato is associated with Makahiki, the Hawaiian new year festival. The first fruits of the harvest, called kāmalui hou, were offered to the gods, and these were typically sweet potatoes and taro.

Hawaiian sweet potato crops faced constant threats. Rats preyed on them during the rainy season, from November to March. Periodic outbreaks of Sphingidae moth caterpillars, cutworms and weevils could greatly damage the crops.

art.text: The most famous Polynesian art forms are the moai, the statues of Rapa Nui, also called Easter Island. They are among the best-known works of Pacific art.
Polynesian art is characteristically ornate and was often meant to contain supernatural power, or mana. Works of art were thought to hold spiritual power and to be able to effect change in the world.

The period beyond 1600 AD brought intense interaction with European explorers, while earlier cultural traditions continued. The collections that European explorers made during the period show that classical Polynesian art was indeed flourishing.

Nan Madol, in the Federated States of Micronesia, was the ceremonial and political seat of the Saudeleur Dynasty, which united Pohnpei's estimated 25,000 people until about 1628. Set apart between the main island of Pohnpei and Temwen Island, it is known for its distinctive megalithic architecture.

Although the moai are often called Easter Island heads, the statues have torsos, and most of them end at the top of the thighs. A small number are complete figures kneeling on bent knees with their hands over their stomachs. Shifting soils have buried some upright moai up to their necks.

war.text: In 1782 the warrior chief who became Kamehameha the Great began a military campaign to unite the Hawaiian Islands. The campaign lasted 15 years and ended with the founding of the Hawaiian Kingdom in 1795.
Oral history from Niutao, an island of Tuvalu, recalls that Tongan warriors invaded it in the late 16th century, in a third and then a fourth invasion. Each time the Tongans were defeated.

Captain James Cook, the first European to encounter the Hawaiian Islands, was killed at Kealakekua Bay on Hawaiʻi Island in 1779, during his third Pacific voyage (1776–1780). He died in a dispute over the taking of a longboat.
Kamehameha built his kingdom with the help of western weapons and advisors, such as John Young and Isaac Davis. With this support he established the Hawaiian Kingdom in 1795.

The Hawaiian Kingdom was established in 1795 when Kamehameha I, then Aliʻi nui of Hawaii, conquered the islands of Oʻahu, Maui, Molokaʻi, and Lānaʻi and unified them under one government. The kingdom was formed with the Battle of Nuʻuanu, which unified all of the main Hawaiian islands under him except Kauaʻi and Niʻihau. Those two joined in 1810.

Kamehameha successfully attacked both Oʻahu and Maui, but he failed to annex Kauaʻi. His attempt was hampered by a storm and by a plague that decimated his army, killing a large part of his fighting men. Kauaʻi's chief swore allegiance to him only in 1810.

literature.text: Rongorongo is a system of glyphs found on Easter Island that looks like writing or proto-writing, discovered in the 19th century. Despite many attempts, no glyph has ever actually been read, and if it does prove to be true writing, it would be one of very few independent inventions of writing in human history.

The Kumulipo is a Hawaiian creation chant first recorded in the 18th century, describing the world being created over a cosmic night. It also contains a genealogy of Hawaiian royalty, created in honor of the chief Kalaninuiamamao.

Māori did not have a writing system before European contact began in 1769, so they relied on oral retellings and recitations memorised and passed down from generation to generation. The main forms of this oral literature were genealogical recital, poetry, and narrative prose.

Hawaiian history was oral history, codified in genealogies and chants that were memorized and passed down in the absence of a written language. Ancient hula, called hula kahiko, was performed before Western encounters with Hawaiʻi and was accompanied by chant and traditional instruments.

About two dozen wooden objects bearing rongorongo inscriptions were collected in the late 19th century, mostly tablets shaped from irregular pieces of wood, including a chieftain's staff and two reimiro ornaments. Oral history suggests only a small elite was ever literate in the script, and that the tablets themselves were considered sacred. Early visitors were told that this elite of ruling families and priests were all kidnapped in the Peruvian slaving raids or died soon afterward in the resulting epidemics.
The Kumulipo was created in honor of the Hawaiian chief Kalaninuiamamao and passed down orally to his daughter, Alapaʻiwahine. Its genealogy continues all the way through to the late 18th century.

Hawaiian kahuna and priests recited the Kumulipo during the makahiki season, in honor of the god Lono. The chant's second section describes the arrival of light and the gods, who watch over the changing of animals into the first humans.

Experts in Māori genealogical recital, poetry, and narrative prose were broadly known as tohunga. Reciting genealogies, or whakapapa, was especially well developed, serving as a kind of time scale linking living people to the gods and legendary heroes of the past.

Authentic rongorongo texts are written in alternating directions, a system called reverse boustrophedon, with glyphs carved as outlines of humans, animals, and plants. On a third of the surviving tablets, the lines of text are inscribed into shallow fluting carved directly into the wood.

In 1770, Spain annexed Easter Island under Captain González de Ahedo, and a treaty of annexation was signed at a ceremony. An undisclosed number of chiefs marked the document with certain characters in their own form of script.

In 1779, Captain James Cook arrived at Kealakekua Bay on the island of Hawaiʻi during the makahiki season and was greeted by Hawaiians reciting the Kumulipo. Some stories say Cook was mistaken for the god Lono, because of the type of sails on his ship and his pale skin tone.

Glyph 67 in rongorongo is thought to depict the Easter Island palm, a tree that vanished from the island's pollen record around 1650, suggesting the script is at least that old. Tablet Q, the sole rongorongo object ever carbon dated, could only be dated to sometime after 1680.

science.text: By the 17th century in central Polynesia, traditional sweet potato cultivars were being replaced with hardier and larger varieties from the Americas. In New Zealand this replacement began later, in the early 19th century.

In 1790, Kīlauea exploded in the deadliest eruption known to have occurred in the modern era in what is now the United States. Up to 5,405 warriors and their families who were marching on the volcano were killed by the eruption.

The prevailing theory for Polynesian sweet potato lineages is the tripartite hypothesis, developed in the 1950s and 1960s. It holds that an original kumara lineage from South America, dated to about 1000 AD, was later superseded by two lineages introduced by Spanish galleons and Portuguese traders around 1500 AD: the Central American camote and the Caribbean batata.

After harvest, kūmara tubers were stored in rua kūmara, subterranean pits with rectangular roofs, sterilised with fire and sealed with small wooden doors to keep out pests. These pits became common across Aotearoa after 1500 AD, and control over them was an important social distinction in classical Maori society.

Inside a rua kūmara, the kūmara were placed on shelves cut into the walls of the pit. They were regularly checked for rot and rotated to keep them dry, and the pits were only packed on dry, sunny days.

Rua kūmara were usually reused, with new posts and roofs added to old structures as they degraded. In the Bay of Plenty, however, the pits were often used for a single season and then backfilled, because of the soft tephra soil.

politics.text: In 1610, the 6th Tuʻi Haʻa Takalaua, Moʻungatonga, created the position of Tuʻi Kanokupolu for Ngata, who was half Samoan. This divided regional rule in Tonga between them. As time went on, the Tuʻi Kanokupolu's power became more and more dominant over Tonga.

In 1767, Captain Samuel Wallis brought HMS Dolphin to Tahiti, and cultural differences led to grave communication errors. A battle followed in Matavai Bay between three hundred war canoes and the ship, which fired on the canoes with muskets, quarterdeck guns and then cannons. Afterward the chief Obera (Purea) ordered peace offerings from her people, and Wallis left on amicable terms on 27 July 1767.

Each year at Muʻa, following the harvest, all countries subject to the Tuʻi Tonga had to bring a gift for the gods, and the Tuʻi Tonga was recognized as the one who received it. This tribute was called the ʻInasi. Captain James Cook witnessed an Inasi ceremony in 1777.

On 28 November 1520, Ferdinand Magellan's expedition entered the ocean he named "Pacific". His ships then sailed north and caught the trade winds, which carried them across the Pacific to the Philippines, where Magellan was killed.

In January 1778, James Cook sighted the Hawaiian Islands on his third voyage, the first documented European contact. When he anchored at Kealakekua Bay, the local people were at first respectful, friendly and accommodating. After a storm damaged a mast and forced the ships back, relations turned hostile, and Cook was among those killed when a dispute led to violence.

In 1595 the Spanish navigator Álvaro de Mendaña reached Pukapuka, the first European contact with the Cook Islands. Pedro Fernández de Quirós made the first European landing on Rakahanga in 1606, calling it Gente Hermosa (Beautiful People).

The name Kanokupolu translates as the "Heart of Upolu", a direct homage to Ngata's Samoan mother. The Tuʻi Kanokupolu dynasty imported many Samoan policies and titles. According to Tongan scholars, this "Samoanized" form of government and custom continues today in the modern Kingdom of Tonga.

The falefā were created as political advisors to the Tongan empire, and at first they kept some hegemony over subject islands. Increasing dissatisfaction led to the assassination of several rulers in succession. Havea I, Havea II and Takalaua, the 23rd Tuʻi Tonga, were all known for their tyrannical rule.

Tahitian society was divided into three major classes: ariʼi, raʼatira and manahune. The ariʼi were relatively few in number, while the manahune made up the bulk of the population. Some manahune played essential roles in society.
The Pōmare Dynasty rose to prominence in the early 1790s. This ruling Tahitian family was aided by the protection of British mercenaries drawn from the mutineers on the Bounty.

When James Cook sighted the Hawaiian Islands in January 1778, even that initial limited contact introduced firearms to Hawaiian warfare. Aided by firearms and ships, Kamehameha I conquered and unified most of the islands in 1795, establishing the Kingdom of Hawaii.

After Kalaniʻōpuʻu died in 1782, his son Kīwalaʻō took his place as first born and ruled the island. Kamehameha I became the religious authority. Some chiefs preferred Kamehameha I, and war broke out, in which Kīwalaʻō was killed at the Battle of Mokuʻōhai.
In AD 1535, Takalaua was assassinated by two foreigners while swimming in the lagoon of Muʻa. His successor, Kauʻulufonua I, pursued the killers all the way to ʻUvea, where he killed them.

The first Europeans reached Tonga in 1616, when the Dutch explorers Willem Schouten and Jacob Le Maire spotted Tongans in a canoe off Niuatoputapu. Abel Tasman passed by the islands on 20 January 1643. These visits were brief and did not significantly change the islands.

Only months after Wallis left Tahiti, the French arrived on 2 April 1768 with the ships Boudeuse and Etoile, captained by Louis-Antoine de Bougainville. European ships brought diseases such as dysentery, smallpox, scarlet fever, typhoid fever, venereal disease and tuberculosis, to which Tahitians had little or no acquired immunity. By 1830 the population of Tahiti had fallen to 15,300 from an estimated 110,000 in 1767.

After Magellan's death, one surviving ship went north hoping to find the westerlies and reach Mexico. Unable to find the right winds, it was forced to return to the East Indies. The other, led by Juan Sebastián Elcano, returned west across the Indian Ocean and achieved the first circumnavigation of the world.

The megalithic floating city of Nan Madol began in 1200 AD and was still being built when European explorers began to arrive around 1600. By around 1800 the city had declined, along with the Saudeleur dynasty. It was abandoned altogether by the 1820s.

philosophy.text: Traditional Hawaiian religion, also known as the kapu system, was polytheistic. It held that spirits live in non-human animals and in natural elements such as the waves and the sky. Among its most prominent deities were Kāne, Kū, Lono and Kanaloa. Breaking a kapu could be punished by death, and during times of war the first two men killed were offered to the gods as sacrifices. The article also says human sacrifice was not unknown.

Hawaiian ecological and agricultural practices were upheld by spiritual beliefs like the lokahi. Scholar Mililani Trask describes it as a triangle with three points: the Creator (Akua), the peoples of the earth (Kanaka Maoli), and the land (ʻaina). All three, she says, have a reciprocal relationship.

In many Polynesian cultures, people believed that a person's errors, called hara or hala, caused illness. Some thought error angered the gods, others that it attracted malevolent gods, and others that the guilt itself made one sick. Special rites could be performed to atone for such errors.

Samoan natives long claimed to be the indigenous people of their islands. They held firmly to the belief that Samoans were birthed from a tear in the heavens (Lagi, Lani), a special creation in Samoa. Linguists and anthropologists theorize instead that migrants from Maritime Southeast Asia arrived approximately 3500 years ago.

Hawaiian religion focused on natural forces such as the tides, the sky and volcanic activity, and on humanity's dependence on nature for subsistence. Its major early gods reflected this. Kāne was the god of sky and creation, Kū of war and male pursuits, Lono of peace, rain and fertility, and Kanaloa of the ocean. Kū was the god worshiped during times of war, and during war the first two men killed were offered to the gods as sacrifices.

Hawaiians, the people of Tikopia in the Solomon Islands, and people on Rarotonga in the Cook Islands believed the sins of the father fall upon the children. A sick child made people suspect the parents of quarreling or misconduct. Social disorder could even cause sterility of land, and harmony was restored only by confession and apology.

In Hawaiian belief, every Native Hawaiian family was considered to have one or more guardian spirits called ʻaumakua. These spirits protected the family. Other notable deities included Laka, Kihawahine, Haumea, Papahānaumoku and, most famously, Pele.

Early Hawaiian historians documented a belief that illness was caused by breaking kapu, or spiritual laws. The sufferer could not be cured until atoning for the transgression, often with the help of a praying priest (kahuna pule) or a healing priest (kahuna lapaʻau). Forgiveness was sought from the gods or from the person in dispute.

Hawaiian scholar Nana Veary wrote in her book Change We Must: My Spiritual Journey that hoʻoponopono was a practice in Ancient Hawaii. She said this is supported by oral histories from contemporary Hawaiian elders. The Hawaiian word hoʻoponopono itself translates simply as correction.

culture.text: Hawaiian religion involved the worship of natural forces and ancestral spirits, and religious rituals accompanied any serious action, whether building a house or going to battle. Three gods were especially prominent: Kāne, god of light and life; Lono, god of harvest and peace; and Kū, god of war.

Polynesian culture developed largely in isolation in the centuries before European contact. Each island group developed politically in its own way, from fully developed kingdoms to constantly warring tribes or family groups, sometimes even within the same valley.
Kū, the god of war, was particularly revered in Hawaii. Places of worship and sacrifice were called heiau, and human sacrifices were sometimes performed at state temples known as luakini.

Ancient Hawaiian society was ruled by local chiefs called aliʻi, who launched wars to extend their influence and defend their communities. It was a caste-based society, and chiefdoms grew until some encompassed whole islands.

Hawaiians combined upland agriculture, ocean fishing, fishponds and gardening systems, supported by spiritual beliefs such as the lokahi. Scholar Mililani Trask describes it as a triangle linking the Creator, Akua; the people, Kanaka Maoli; and the land, the ʻaina.

Polynesia divides into East and West cultural groups. West Polynesian culture, in Tonga, Samoa and surrounding islands, was shaped by high populations and had strong institutions of marriage and well-developed judicial, monetary and trading traditions.
